assessment.nobel_worthiness: Flat bands at the magic angle, correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform for strongly correlated quantum matter, in a material whose existence as a clean 2D crystal once surprised theorists. Prediction from a continuum band-structure model met a decisive experiment, which is the pairing of theory and measurement I value most.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands and the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group found the correlated insulator and superconductivity in 2018. Andrei's STM work on flat bands and Van Hove singularities in twisted layers is an early experimental strand. Credit is clear for MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. The third seat is arguable between Bistritzer and Andrei, and I defer to colleagues on that.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have reproduced the phase diagram, and the field has grown enormously in under a decade. The microscopic nature of the superconductivity is still debated, but the core discovery is robust.
uncertainties: Whether the third place should go to Bistritzer or Andrei is unresolved.
The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled.
Sample-to-sample variation in twist angle and strain complicates reproducibility.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators brought a new classification of band structure into materials physics, with protected surface and edge states, and changed how the community searches for materials. It is a conceptual change as well as a family of materials, and it is quantitatively testable with ARPES, which I appreciate.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 quantum spin Hall insulator, Molenkamp's group observed the edge channels in HgTe wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Hasan's group gave the first 3D ARPES evidence. Leaving Mele out of a Kane-led theory seat is hard. Several others, such as Zhang, Fu and Moore, are not in the credited list. The configuration is contested.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by many groups across 2D and 3D materials, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, even somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Mele's omission from the proposed trio is a fairness concern.
The 3D discovery has several claimants outside the supplied names.
Applications remain limited compared with the conceptual impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is a controlled, quantitative framework for the Mott transition and correlated metals. Combined with DFT it handles real materials and spectra, so it is a theory that is directly tied to measurement. It is a major methodological advance.
assessment.attribution: Georges and Kotliar built the modern DMFT framework and its extension to realistic materials. Vollhardt, together with Metzner, introduced the infinite-dimensions limit that underlies it. Metzner is not in the credited names, so the allocation of the foundational credit is incomplete. Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt is a defensible trio from the supplied strings.
assessment.maturity: Used for over 30 years with many independent implementations and benchmarks. Its limits, such as momentum dependence, are well understood. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: Metzner's role in the infinite-dimension limit is not covered by the supplied names.
The prize would honour a method more than a discovery, which some colleagues may consider less compelling.
I have not independently checked the credit chronology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and coherent tunnelling in crystalline MgO barriers are the basis of modern hard-disk read heads and MRAM. Spin-dependent tunnelling and symmetry filtering are well understood from first-principles calculations, so theory and experiment agree. The physics is clear and the impact large, although GMR was already recognised in 2007.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in amorphous barriers in 1995. Parkin and Yuasa independently demonstrated giant TMR in MgO in 2004, following the Butler and Mathon theoretical predictions, which are not among the credited names. The three selected names cover the main experimental strands, but Miyazaki has an equally strong claim.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with independent confirmation from several laboratories and years of industrial use. Timing is later than ideal, so recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Miyazaki is left out although he has an equally strong claim to the amorphous-barrier discovery.
Theory predictions by Butler and Mathon are not credited in the supplied list.
Overlap with the earlier GMR prize may reduce its novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third class of collinear magnetic order, with compensated moments but spin-split bands. It is a symmetry-based classification with real consequences for spintronics, and it sits close to my own field. It also re-reads known materials such as MnTe and RuO2.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth are the clear authors of the 2022 classification and its development. Credit is concentrated and uncontested in the supplied list, although independent earlier symmetry insights in the literature may deserve acknowledgement.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation by ARPES and spin-splitting measurements in MnTe and CrSb has appeared only in the last few years. The picture is stabilising but recognition is probably early. Some claims, such as those for RuO2, remain disputed.
uncertainties: The ground state of RuO2 as an altermagnet is disputed.
Application impact is still prospective.
Prior symmetry-based work may complicate priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of 39 K superconductivity in MgB2 and of high-Tc superconductivity in iron-based pnictides produced new classes of superconductors with unexpected multiband character. First-principles electronic-structure theory explained the MgB2 electron-phonon pairing quantitatively. These are real discoveries in materials physics.
assessment.attribution: Akimitsu discovered MgB2 superconductivity in 2001 and Hosono the iron-based family in 2008, which started with the LaFeAsO(F) report. These are two separate discoveries, so a joint prize would join two compound discoveries and the committee may prefer only one. The two named people have a clear claim to their respective parts.
assessment.maturity: Both are mature and independently confirmed. The mechanism of iron-based superconductivity is still debated, and applications are modest.
uncertainties: The two discoveries are distinct and a joint prize may be hard to justify.
The pairing mechanism for the iron-based compounds is not settled.
The Nobel significance relative to cuprates is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantized conductance in ballistic point contacts gave a clean, textbook demonstration of Landauer transport, and created the foundation of mesoscopic physics including later electron optics and spin-qubit devices. The result is simple, exact and beautifully quantitative.
assessment.attribution: van Wees and Wharam published independent, near-simultaneous observations in 1988, with Pepper's Cambridge group responsible for the Wharam work. The credit is clear between the two groups. Landauer's theory, and the Cambridge team contributions of others, are not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and universally reproduced, so recognition is long overdue, if anything. The interest in it is now fundamental rather than frontier.
uncertainties: The Nobel committee may view it as too old and specialised.
Theoretical credit to Landauer and Büttiker is not covered by the credited names.
Pepper's role in the Wharam paper needs checking against the other Cambridge co-authors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect gives quantized Hall resistance without an external field in a magnetic topological insulator, a new state with potential metrology use. The theoretical prediction and an experimental realisation are directly connected, which I like.
assessment.attribution: Fang and Dai, with Zhang and others, made the 2010 and 2013 predictions, and Xue's group first observed the effect in Cr-doped (Bi,Sb)2Te3 in 2013. The theory and experiment pairing is sensible, but it overlaps strongly with the topological insulator prize candidate, and other theorists such as Haldane are outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation exists from several laboratories, but the quantization temperatures are still low and the effect is fragile. It would likely be recognised as part of a broader topological prize rather than on its own.
uncertainties: It overlaps with candidate B009 and may be better bundled with it than recognised separately.
Haldane's earlier model and Zhang's prediction are not in the credited list.
Low operating temperature limits technology relevance.
